David Bontemps, porteur de mélodies viva: David Bontemps, carrier of living melodies
Découvrez la musique classique haïtienne: Discover Haitian classical music with David Bontemps in Montréal! He unites classical forms and Haitian influences for a vibrant art.
Le compositeur David Bontemps, avec la p: Composer David Bontemps with the score of Le Flambeau. Photographer: Kevin Calixte
Le mois de mai est celui du patrimoine h: May is Haitian Heritage Month, and Flag Day takes place on May 18, a national event celebrated by the diaspora. This time, for the occasion, I invite you to discover a little-known art form: Haitian classical music. I hope you are as intrigued as I was when I first heard about it!
En 2023, j’ai eu l’occasion d’assister à: In 2023, I had the chance to attend the world premiere of Le Flambeau, an opera by Haitian composer David Bontemps, at the Salle Pierre-Mercure, which was packed. As someone of Haitian origin myself, I particularly appreciated the work and its window onto the country’s culture. The friends who came with me enjoyed the performance just as much, even though they don’t share the same culture. It was a very special moment to share.
L’an dernier, j’ai eu l’occasion d’enten: Last year, I had the opportunity to hear the composer again, this time playing works by Haitian classical composers on the piano. I wanted to learn more about the subject and to share this music. This is the result.
Nous rencontrons le pianiste et composit:
We meet pianist and composer David Bontemps at his home in Montréal. Outside, the air is crisp, but the idea of talking about Haitian classical music with the musician warms the soul and the ears. David hums a tune, convinced that we would easily recognize the melody. While the song is indeed familiar to me, I couldn’t say where it comes from, or what it’s called. “That’s Nibo by Ludovic Lamothe, which won first prize at Carnival in 1934. People don’t know who wrote it, it’s part of popular culture, but it’s a Haitian classical piece.”

Haitian classical music is a little-known cultural heritage. Its repertoire consists of pieces composed using the codes of European classical music, but that incorporate Haitian influences in their themes, rhythms, titles and lyrics. These pieces, which have been emerging since the 19th century, have unfortunately been recorded very little – something David Bontemps is remedying, as he performs them and composes his own.
C’est dans sa maison d’enfance, à Port-A: It was in his childhood home in Port-au-Prince that music first found David. “It was pretty eclectic. There was a lot of classical music, my father listened to a lot of old jazz, like Louis Armstrong, Nat King Cole, and then kompa.” At the home of young David’s grandparents stood an out-of-tune upright piano, where all the cousins would tinker.
En Haïti, l'année 1986 marque la fin de: In Haiti, 1986 marked the end of the Duvalier dictatorship, which had lasted 29 years. During their rule, music and the arts were censored, to prevent works unfavourable to the political regime. A resurgence of classical music and of Haitian chansonniers followed. Eventually, local Haitian popular music, with voices like Emeline Michel and Sidon Joseph, took off across the country.
Comme c’est souvent le cas pour les pare: As is often the case for parents who can afford it, David’s enrolled the siblings in music lessons. David chose the piano. “I liked it, and little by little it became something I was more and more interested in,” the musician says. Alongside his studies, he trained for more than 10 years under a master, the distinguished composer Serge Villedrouin.
« Il m’a tout appris, et réappris ». Son: “He taught me everything, and taught it to me again.” His teacher introduced him to the repertoire of Haitian classical composers. He remembers the first piece he learned: Paillettes, by Férère Laguerre… “He was a fairly modern composer, the piece is bitonal, meaning the right hand is in E-flat and the left in E minor, and it’s in counterpoint. So, really modern!”
Ce n’est alors que le début pour le jeun: This was only the beginning for the young pianist. He then met other comrades, as he calls them: the Haitian composers Ludovic Lamothe, Justin Élie and Carmen Brouard. He also discovered Haiti’s school of classical composition, as well as the Sainte-Trinité music school, an important institution in the capital that trains the next generation of musicians. The philharmonic concerts presented by the students left a strong impression on the pianist. “The halls are packed, people come. They appreciate that the children are learning Bach and Beethoven, but when there’s a piece by a Haitian composer, it vibrates very strongly.”
Si elle ne parvient qu’à certaines oreil: Though it reaches only some ears, Haitian classical music is not a new genre. “Not only has it always existed, but it is dynamic and alive,” says the pianist. “Young people who play a so-called classical instrument now are much more aware [of the existence of these composers] than in my day,” explains David, who has met several young musicians and composers in Haiti.
En 2001, David Bontemps obtient son dipl: In 2001, David Bontemps earned his law degree from the State University of Haiti in Port-au-Prince. The following year, he settled in Montréal to pursue law studies at Université de Montréal. But the call of music remained, and endured. In 2002, renowned professor and musicologist Claude Dauphin, also of Haitian origin, introduced him as “the next generation of Haitian composers.” Since then, David Bontemps has never stopped playing, composing, recording and performing the music that drives him.
« C’est un langage universel. Les oreill: “It’s a universal language. Ears have no eyelids,” says the pianist. “Even when we sleep, or when we’re babies, we are steeped in the sounds around us. When we speak, whatever the language, we always have the accent of childhood.”
Voilà qui ne cesse d’inspirer sa musique: This continues to inspire his music and his playing. At the piano, the composer reproduces what he hears. “It’s really a challenge to notate certain rhythms, it’s very complex!”
Le système de notation moderne avec port: The modern system of notation with staves, widely used today, originated in Europe. “My teacher did it on purpose, he wouldn’t give me the keys and would say ‘try to figure it out yourself.’ That piqued my curiosity even more,” the pianist says.
Il voit dans son pays une source créatri: He sees in his country an inexhaustible creative source. “The nationalist fibre, these are beautiful sources, which allow you to enter into the traditions of a people, of a nation, to dissect them and conceptualize them. At the same time, it allows for openness. These sources are ambassadors of the culture they come from.”
Comme n’importe quelle musique, celle qu: Like any music, music that expresses an attachment to a particular nation is steeped in what surrounds it. “Inevitably there will be interpenetration with other modes of expression, other genres, other cultures, other eras,” explains the composer. Haitian classical music is born of this alloy. Originally, these were pairings imposed following France’s colonization of the territory. In 1804, Haiti won its independence through a revolution, and became the first independent nation founded by former slaves.
Pourtant, les siècles n'ont pu effacer l: Yet the centuries have not been able to erase the traces of colonization. The country inherited the systems and customs of the colonizers, still in place today. The Haitian constitution, moreover, was written in French, which remains one of the country’s official languages today. Haitian literature, very rich, is written in a creolized French – in its words, but also in its images, David notes.
Comment s’épanouir et faire advenir ce q: “How do we flourish and bring forth what makes us who we are through modes of expression that we inherited and did not choose?” David wonders, speaking of classical music. He brings up the German-Haitian composer Werner Jaegerhuber (1900-1953), some of whose works he has performed. “He studied music in Germany, he even became a professor and conductor there.” With the rise of Nazism, Werner Jaegerhuber fled the country and returned to live in Haiti with his family. “The first thing he did was go out into the streets and notate traditional Vodou music.” Drawing on its themes, he composed several melodies. “He even wrote a Mass in Latin with Vodou themes. The bishop, a foreigner, nearly excommunicated him. It devastated him, he died a few years later,” David says.
Les traditions haïtiennes et occidentale: Haitian and Western traditions are equal in worth, David believes. He mentions rara music, associated with Vodou. “It carries a message, a wisdom, you just have to open your eyes. If you present the same [music, the same stories], but attribute them to another people, people are amazed,” he laments.
Lors d’un concert donné dans un CHSLD, D: At a concert given in a long-term care home (CHSLD), David witnessed a butterfly release, in reference to an Indigenous legend. If you confide a secret to the silent insect, it is supposed to go to the creator to grant the wish. “We have almost the same legend in Vodou tales, ‘Papa Loko.’”
Sons, syllabes, idées, mots, visions du: Sounds, syllables, ideas, words, worldviews, colours, figures – everything is called upon to be interpreted, to be joined together. Harmony, musical here, can also happen on a personal level. “We ourselves, descendants of colonized peoples, must make peace with the components of our past. It’s still very painful for many,” he confides. He hopes his compatriots won’t disparage one part of their identity in favour of another.
Au sujet des effets dévastateurs de la c: On the devastating effects of colonization that endure, the musician draws a parallel with residential schools for Indigenous children in Canada. As a child, he himself attended a school run by a religious congregation. “Now I know what it was: an ethnocide. When you can’t physically kill a people, you kill their essence, their soul, their culture, their language, their beliefs, their religion, their arts. When you can’t kill that, you make it seem inferior so that, eventually, people abandon it. That’s what happened to us. Now we don’t even need missionaries to do it, we do it ourselves with gusto. That’s a wound,” says the composer, speaking of the hold religion has on many Haitians. “You could say religion so white!”
« Il y a beaucoup de mots à poser sur le: “There are a lot of words to be put to the wounds we carry,” the musician says. That is where, in his view, art can play a role. “I hope that this kind of music, this alloy, this blending, this hybridization – can make that possible.”
La haine de soi, insidieuse, inculquée d: Self-hatred, insidious, first instilled by the occupier, is one of these wounds. It’s what drives people to demonize the folkloric aspects of a people, David believes. “What do we do with our compatriots who practise Vodou?” He says he himself was lucky to have been raised in a family that did not belittle this ancestral practice, which is far from the case for everyone. “Even so, it was a long road before I recognized in it a source of interest like any other – before I saw that it’s a source that belongs to me, and that people have preserved under the conditions we know.”
Il raconte à ce sujet une anecdote surve: He recounts an anecdote on the subject from when he was performing Offrandes Vodouesques, a cycle of 24 melodies by Werner Jaegerhuber, with soprano Chantale Lavigne, at the historic Bon Pasteur chapel in Montréal. “I played very badly that evening.” “But at the end, a white-haired man with a cane, who had left Haiti a very long time ago, came to see us with tears in his eyes. It was powerful, because a Haitian man of his age doesn’t cry in public. He said thank you, thank you, because he had always grown up and lived believing it was diabolical music, and now it touched him.”
